claim: Deviant stimuli enhanced tactile detection in mice.
source: We found that deviant stimuli enhanced tactile detection and were encoded in L2/3 neural tuning.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing increased detection rates for deviant-containing stimuli in head-fixed detection task (Figure 3).

claim: Deviant stimuli were encoded in L2/3 neural tuning.
source: We found that deviant stimuli enhanced tactile detection and were encoded in L2/3 neural tuning.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing heterogeneous change coefficients in L2/3 neurons (Figure 7).

claim: Weak optogenetic drive changed which L6 neurons were sensory responsive without affecting overall firing rates in L6 or L2/3.
source: To test the contribution of L6, we applied weak optogenetic drive that changed which L6 neurons were sensory responsive, without affecting overall firing rates in L6 or L2/3.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data showing ensemble shuffling (Figure 5) and electrophysiology showing no change in mean firing rates (Figure 4).

claim: Weak L6 optogenetic stimulation selectively suppressed behavioral sensitivity to deviant stimuli without impacting baseline performance.
source: This stimulation selectively suppressed behavioral sensitivity to deviant stimuli, without impacting baseline performance.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing loss of deviant-driven slowing in Gap Crossing with Deviation (Figure 2) and loss of deviant benefit in head-fixed detection (Figure 3) while baseline performance remained intact.

claim: Weak L6 optogenetic stimulation eliminated deviance encoding in L2/3.
source: This stimulation also eliminated deviance encoding in L2/3 but did not impair basic stimulus responses across layers.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing sharpening of change coefficient distribution in L2/3 during weak L6 drive (Figure 9).

claim: Weak L6 optogenetic stimulation did not impair basic stimulus responses across layers.
source: This stimulation also eliminated deviance encoding in L2/3 but did not impair basic stimulus responses across layers.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing no significant changes in sensory-evoked firing rates in RS neurons across layers (Figure 4).

claim: Strong L6 drive inhibited firing and suppressed overall sensory function.
source: In contrast, stronger L6 drive inhibited firing and suppressed overall sensory function.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing reduced Gap Crossing probability (Figure 1) and electrophysiological data showing reduced sensory gain (Figure 4a).

claim: Specific ensembles of stimulus-driven L6 neurons are required to form neocortical predictions.
source: These findings indicate that, despite their sparse activity, specific ensembles of stimulus-driven L6 neurons are required to form neocortical predictions, and to realize their behavioral benefit.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of behavioral deficits, loss of L2/3 deviance encoding, and L6 ensemble shuffling under weak optogenetic drive.

claim: The six-layered architecture of mammalian neocortex emerged relatively late in evolution.
source: The six-layered architecture of mammalian neocortex emerged relatively late in evolution.
evidence: Statement based on established evolutionary neuroscience knowledge.

claim: A commonly proposed function of neocortex is to form dynamic predictive models that include expectations of incoming stimuli and contextually appropriate actions.
source: A commonly proposed function of neocortex is to form dynamic predictive models that include expectations of incoming stimuli and contextually appropriate actions.
evidence: Statement based on established theoretical frameworks in neuroscience.

claim: When identical sensory stimuli are repeated and then a 'deviant' occurs, neocortical neurons often fire differently than they would to the deviant in isolation, or after its repetition.
source: When identical sensory stimuli are repeated and then a 'deviant' occurs, neocortical neurons often fire differently than they would to the deviant in isolation, or after its repetition (Chater et al., 2006; Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Signatures of deviance detection are found in visual areas.
source: Signatures of this computation are found in visual (Courchesne et al., 1975), auditory (Tiitinen et al., 1994; Ulanovsky et al., 2003), and language- processing (Kutas and Hillyard, 1980) areas.
evidence: Supported by citation to Courchesne et al., 1975.

claim: Signatures of deviance detection are found in auditory areas.
source: Signatures of this computation are found in visual (Courchesne et al., 1975), auditory (Tiitinen et al., 1994; Ulanovsky et al., 2003), and language- processing (Kutas and Hillyard, 1980) areas.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tiitinen et al., 1994 and Ulanovsky et al., 2003.

claim: Signatures of deviance detection are found in language-processing areas.
source: Signatures of this computation are found in visual (Courchesne et al., 1975), auditory (Tiitinen et al., 1994; Ulanovsky et al., 2003), and language- processing (Kutas and Hillyard, 1980) areas.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kutas and Hillyard, 1980.

claim: Change detection is typically studied as the increase in firing rates elicited by deviant stimuli following stimulus-specific adaptation.
source: Such change detection is typically studied as the increase in firing rates elicited by deviant stimuli following stimulus-specific adaptation (Movshon and Lennie, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Movshon and Lennie, 1979.

claim: Stimulus-tuned neurons along the afferent pathway adapt to repeated stimulation.
source: Stimulus-tuned neurons along the afferent pathway, including at thalamocortical synapses, adapt to repeated stimulation (Chung et al., 2002; Katz et al., 2006; Khatri and Simons, 2007) and subsequent deviant stimuli activate new pools of less adapted neurons, leading to increased neocortical drive.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2002; Katz et al., 2006; Khatri and Simons, 2007.

claim: Neocortically-represented factors such as stimulus context, history, and expectation influence sensory responses.
source: However, in addition to such bottom-up adaptation mechanisms, neocortically-represented factors such as stimulus context, history, and expectation (Knierim and van Essen, 1992; Chelazzi et al., 1993; Reynolds et al., 2000; Maunsell and Treue, 2006) also influence sensory responses, supporting the hypothesis that neocortical representations could be key to deviant processing.
evidence: Supported by citations to Knierim and van Essen, 1992; Chelazzi et al., 1993; Reynolds et al., 2000; Maunsell and Treue, 2006.

claim: Layers 2/3 are a leading candidate for the representation of more complex information.
source: While likely all neocortical layers contribute to model implementation, layers 2/3 (L2/3) are a leading candidate for the representation of more complex information.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple cited studies showing L2/3 properties.

claim: L2/3 are typically the first to express receptive-field plasticity in response to sensory change, prior to L4.
source: These supragranular layers are typically the first to express receptive-field plasticity in response to sensory change, prior to L4 (Diamond et al., 1994), and are more susceptible to modulation by shifts in attentional state than deeper layers (Hyvärinen et al., 1980).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diamond et al., 1994.

claim: L2/3 are more susceptible to modulation by shifts in attentional state than deeper layers.
source: These supragranular layers are typically the first to express receptive-field plasticity in response to sensory change, prior to L4 (Diamond et al., 1994), and are more susceptible to modulation by shifts in attentional state than deeper layers (Hyvärinen et al., 1980).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hyvärinen et al., 1980.

claim: In primary somatosensory and visual neocortices, L2/3 receptive fields can encode specific temporal stimulus patterns.
source: Further, in primary somatosensory and visual neocortices, L2/3 receptive fields can encode specific temporal stimulus patterns (Estebanez et al., 2016; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968), and can integrate multiple types of information (e.g. motor and sensory signals) and the mismatch in their alignment (Zmarz and Keller, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Estebanez et al., 2016 and Hubel and Wiesel, 1968.

claim: L2/3 can integrate multiple types of information (e.g. motor and sensory signals) and the mismatch in their alignment.
source: Further, in primary somatosensory and visual neocortices, L2/3 receptive fields can encode specific temporal stimulus patterns (Estebanez et al., 2016; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968), and can integrate multiple types of information (e.g. motor and sensory signals) and the mismatch in their alignment (Zmarz and Keller, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zmarz and Keller, 2016.

claim: Layer 6 is well positioned to contribute to the neocortical implementation of predictive models.
source: Layer 6 (L6) is also well positioned to contribute to the neocortical implementation of predictive models, as it integrates lemniscal thalamic, long-range cortico-cortical, and modulatory inputs (Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Zhang and Deschênes, 1998; Thomson, 2010; Zhang et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations describing L6 connectivity: Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Zhang and Deschênes, 1998; Thomson, 2010; Zhang et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2014.

claim: Corticothalamic L6 neurons in primary visual and somatosensory neocortex are sparsely sensory driven.
source: Corticothalamic L6 neurons (CT) in primary visual and somatosensory neocortex are sparsely sensory driven (Lee et al., 2008) with selective receptive fields (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014) and can robustly modulate sensory gain through an intracortical pathway (Olsen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: Corticothalamic L6 neurons have selective receptive fields.
source: Corticothalamic L6 neurons (CT) in primary visual and somatosensory neocortex are sparsely sensory driven (Lee et al., 2008) with selective receptive fields (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014) and can robustly modulate sensory gain through an intracortical pathway (Olsen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vélez-Fort et al., 2014.

claim: Corticothalamic L6 neurons can robustly modulate sensory gain through an intracortical pathway.
source: Corticothalamic L6 neurons (CT) in primary visual and somatosensory neocortex are sparsely sensory driven (Lee et al., 2008) with selective receptive fields (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014) and can robustly modulate sensory gain through an intracortical pathway (Olsen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2012.

claim: L6 mediates modulation of visual receptive fields by stimulus context.
source: This prediction is supported by L6-mediated modulation of visual receptive fields by stimulus context (Bolz and Gilbert, 1986), by the relay of information from head-motion into V1 via L6 (Vélez-Fort et al., 2018), and by preferential involvement of deep cortical layers in top-down sensory processing (Kok et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bolz and Gilbert, 1986.

claim: L6 relays information from head-motion into V1.
source: This prediction is supported by L6-mediated modulation of visual receptive fields by stimulus context (Bolz and Gilbert, 1986), by the relay of information from head-motion into V1 via L6 (Vélez-Fort et al., 2018), and by preferential involvement of deep cortical layers in top-down sensory processing (Kok et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vélez-Fort et al., 2018.

claim: Deep cortical layers are preferentially involved in top-down sensory processing.
source: This prediction is supported by L6-mediated modulation of visual receptive fields by stimulus context (Bolz and Gilbert, 1986), by the relay of information from head-motion into V1 via L6 (Vélez-Fort et al., 2018), and by preferential involvement of deep cortical layers in top-down sensory processing (Kok et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kok et al., 2016.

claim: Strong L6 drive reduced the likelihood of successful Gap Crossing from ~75% to ~50%.
source: Strong L6 drive led to a non-specific sensory deficit, reducing the likelihood of successful Gap Crossing from ~75% to ~50% (p<0.01, Figure 1b,c), but had no detectable effect on the whisking pattern of the mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1b,c with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: Strong L6 drive had no detectable effect on the whisking pattern of mice.
source: Strong L6 drive led to a non-specific sensory deficit, reducing the likelihood of successful Gap Crossing from ~75% to ~50% (p<0.01, Figure 1b,c), but had no detectable effect on the whisking pattern of the mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by whisking analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In true change trials, mice slowed their approach after platform retraction.
source: In the true change condition, but in neither of the sham conditions, mice slowed their approach (Figure 2c, p<0.005 change vs. only before, and p<0.01 change vs. only after, rank sum), presumably to precisely re-locate the target before crossing, showing that mice perceive and react to the sensory deviant.
evidence: Supported by behavioral trajectory data in Figure 2c with statistical significance.

claim: Mice perceive and react to sensory deviants in the Gap Crossing with Deviation task.
source: In the true change condition, but in neither of the sham conditions, mice slowed their approach (Figure 2c, p<0.005 change vs. only before, and p<0.01 change vs. only after, rank sum), presumably to precisely re-locate the target before crossing, showing that mice perceive and react to the sensory deviant.
evidence: Inferred from the differential behavioral response to true change vs. sham change conditions.

claim: Weak L6 drive removed the deceleration associated with platform position deviants.
source: We next tested whether the weaker L6 optogenetic drive (<1 mW) would impair this change detection behavior, and found that it removed the extra sampling time that platform motion would otherwise generate (p<0.001 laser vs. control, N = 317 trials, Figure 2d,e, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2d,e showing loss of deceleration with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Weak L6 drive did not affect behavior when the target platform was static.
source: Weak L6 drive did not affect behavior when the target platform was static (p=0.9, N = 751 trials, Figure 2f,g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2f,g showing no significant difference (p=0.9).

claim: Weak L6 drive slightly increased the overall likelihood of crossing.
source: The weaker drive also slightly increased the overall likelihood of crossing (Figure 1d, same analysis as Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Gap Crossing is sensitive to changes in sensory function.
source: Gap Crossing is sensitive to changes in sensory function (Celikel and Sakmann, 2007; Chaudhary and Rema, 2018), the maintenance of regular Gap Crossing behavior in the static platform condition indicates that weak L6 CT drive did not impact basic sensory function, but did impact change detection.
evidence: Supported by citations to Celikel and Sakmann, 2007 and Chaudhary and Rema, 2018.

claim: Weak L6 CT drive did not impact basic sensory function but did impact change detection.
source: Gap Crossing is sensitive to changes in sensory function (Celikel and Sakmann, 2007; Chaudhary and Rema, 2018), the maintenance of regular Gap Crossing behavior in the static platform condition indicates that weak L6 CT drive did not impact basic sensory function, but did impact change detection.
evidence: Inferred from the selective effect on deviant trials but not baseline trials.

claim: Platform position deviants in Gap Crossing likely result from changes in multiple sensory parameters including amplitude of vibrissal contact deflections.
source: Detecting a sudden change in platform position in the Gap Crossing with Deviation experiment likely results from a combination of multiple sensory parameters that change because of the changed position of the vibrissa contacts. Previous high-speed videography studies under the same experimental conditions showed that these parameters include a change in amplitude of vibrissal contact deflections (Voigts et al., 2015), as well as other parameters such as relative timing (Voigts et al., 2015), and likely deflection angles (Knutsen et al., 2008; Ritt et al., 2008), assymetry (Dominiak et al., 2019), time course of the torque (Pammer et al., 2013), and vibrations (Ritt et al., 2008; Lottem and Azouz, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies characterizing vibrissal mechanics.

claim: Deviants increased the detection rate for threshold level stimuli in head-fixed detection task.
source: A subset of these trains contained direction deviants (Figure 3a), though mice were not trained to report the presence of a deviant. Deviants increased the detection rate for threshold level stimuli (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Weak L6 drive removed the behavioral benefit of direction deviants in head-fixed detection.
source: Weak L6 drive removed this effect but had no impact on detection of stimuli containing no deviant.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3b showing loss of deviant benefit under laser condition.

claim: Weak L6 drive had no impact on detection of stimuli containing no deviant.
source: Weak L6 drive removed this effect but had no impact on detection of stimuli containing no deviant.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3b showing no change in baseline detection.

claim: Weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deflection direction in L6.
source: We also observed that weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deflection direction in L6 and of deviant stimuli in L2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by imaging and electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deviant stimuli in L2/3.
source: We also observed that weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deflection direction in L6 and of deviant stimuli in L2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Strong L6 CT optogenetic activation recruits trans-laminar inhibition and reduces neocortical sensory gain in V1.
source: We tested mice on the Gap Crossing task under two conditions, strong L6 CT optogenetic activation (>2 mW power) that recruits trans-laminar inhibition and reduces neocortical sensory gain in V1 (Olsen et al., 2012), or weak L6 drive (<1 mW) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2012.

claim: Strong optogenetic drive of L6 reduces sensory gain in SI.
source: Prior studies have shown that strong L6 drive reduces sensory gain (Olsen et al., 2012; Denman and Contreras, 2015) in V1, and we observed analogous suppression in SI when we drove L6 with the strong optogenetic stimulus (Figure 4a, acute laminar probe recording).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4a and citations to Olsen et al., 2012 and Denman and Contreras, 2015.

claim: L6 neurons were sparsely sensory responsive, with only ~13% being phasically sensory driven.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Thomson, 2010; Lee et al., 2008; Swadlow and Hicks, 1996), L6 neurons were sparsely sensory responsive, as only 18 (RS and FS) of 139 (~13%) were phasically sensory driven.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and citations to Thomson, 2010; Lee et al., 2008; Swadlow and Hicks, 1996.

claim: Driven L6 neurons showed only small vibrissa-driven increases in their activity.
source: Further, driven L6 neurons were also sparse in their response rates, showing only small vibrissa-driven increases in their activity (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Weak L6 drive did not impact sensory-evoked firing rates in RS from any layer.
source: In contrast to stronger drive, this stimulus did not impact sensory-evoked firing rates in RS from any layer (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Weak L6 drive caused a modest decrease in sensory responses in L4 FS.
source: The only significant impact on sensory responses was a modest decrease in sensory responses in L4 FS (31.7 vs. 24.6 Hz median peak rates, p=0.001, Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4b with statistical significance p=0.001.

claim: A small increase in firing rates in non-sensory-responsive L6 FS was observed with weak L6 drive.
source: A small increase in firing rates in non-sensory-responsive L6 FS was also observed (Figure 4b, p=0.02 sign-rank, laser - control firing rates, N = 37).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4b with statistical significance p=0.02.

claim: Increased activity in L6 FS presumably offset the direct effects of optogenetic drive in L6 RS, keeping L6 RS firing rates at baseline level.
source: Increased activity in these L6 FS presumably offset the direct effects of optogenetic drive in L6 RS, keeping L6 RS firing rates at a baseline level (p=0.18, N = 89, signed rank).
evidence: Inferred from the balance between excitatory drive and inhibitory compensation, supported by non-significant change in L6 RS rates (p=0.18).

claim: In L2/3 and L5 RS, transient suppression was evident after optogenetic stimulus onset, but rates returned to baseline prior to sensory stimulation.
source: In L2/3 and L5 RS, transient suppression was evident after optogenetic stimulus onset, but rates returned to baseline prior to sensory stimulation.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing temporal dynamics of firing rates.

claim: Weak optogenetic drive did not change the mean population response of L6 to sensory input.
source: Optogenetic drive did not significantly change the mean population response of L6 to sensory input, ranksum test, CI via bootstrap of median.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5f with statistical test.

claim: Individual L6 cells showed significant facilitation or suppression of vibrissa-evoked responses during optogenetic drive.
source: However, individual L6 cells showed significant facilitation or suppression of vibrissa-evoked responses during optogenetic drive.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Optogenetic L6 activation shifted the identity of the activated ensemble.
source: Optogenetic L6 activation did not change the overall output from L6, but shifted the identity of the activated ensemble (p<0.001 IQR vs. shuffled control), regardless of whether cells were classified as vibrissa-driven in the control (red) or in the laser (blue) condition.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5h with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Of L6 cells that were sensory responsive in the laser condition, 25.0% were significantly facilitated and 23.9% suppressed.
source: Of cells that were sensory responsive in the laser condition, 25.0% were significantly facilitated, 23.9% suppressed, and of cells sensory responsive in the control condition, 10.9% were facilitated, 32.9% suppressed.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Of L6 cells that were sensory responsive in the control condition, 10.9% were facilitated and 32.9% suppressed.
source: Of cells that were sensory responsive in the laser condition, 25.0% were significantly facilitated, 23.9% suppressed, and of cells sensory responsive in the control condition, 10.9% were facilitated, 32.9% suppressed.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Variations in stimulus amplitude without deviants were not encoded in the mean firing rates of L4 RS cells.
source: Variations in stimulus amplitude (without deviants) were not encoded in the mean firing rates of layer 4 (L4) or L2/3 RS cells (L4 N = 37 RS; spike count difference between larger and smaller stimuli, signed rank p=0.221, 95% confidence interval (CI): [−0.22, 0, 0.002], L2/3 N = 94, p=0.201, CI:[−0.009,–0.003,0], Figure 6a–c).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6a-c with statistical tests showing non-significance.

claim: Variations in stimulus amplitude without deviants were not encoded in the mean firing rates of L2/3 RS cells.
source: Variations in stimulus amplitude (without deviants) were not encoded in the mean firing rates of layer 4 (L4) or L2/3 RS cells (L4 N = 37 RS; spike count difference between larger and smaller stimuli, signed rank p=0.221, 95% confidence interval (CI): [−0.22, 0, 0.002], L2/3 N = 94, p=0.201, CI:[−0.009,–0.003,0], Figure 6a–c).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6a-c with statistical tests showing non-significance.

claim: Small variations in overall stimulus strength were not reliably encoded in SI.
source: Small variations in overall stimulus strength were therefore not reliably encoded in SI.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of significant encoding in L4 and L2/3 RS cells.

claim: Neither L2/3 nor L4 neurons systematically increased their overall firing rates for deviants when amplitude increases and decreases were grouped together.
source: While individual neurons displayed such sensitivity to deviation (Figure 6d), neither L2/3 nor L4 neurons systematically increased their overall firing rates for deviants when amplitude increases and decreases were grouped together (Figure 6e), showing that our stimulus design avoided pre-cortical stimulus-specific adaptation (Movshon and Lennie, 1979).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6e showing no systematic rate increase.

claim: The stimulus design avoided pre-cortical stimulus-specific adaptation.
source: While individual neurons displayed such sensitivity to deviation (Figure 6d), neither L2/3 nor L4 neurons systematically increased their overall firing rates for deviants when amplitude increases and decreases were grouped together (Figure 6e), showing that our stimulus design avoided pre-cortical stimulus-specific adaptation (Movshon and Lennie, 1979).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of overall rate increase for deviants, with reference to Movshon and Lennie, 1979.

claim: L4 neurons consistently showed positive change coefficients, firing more spikes for deviant increases and fewer for decreases.
source: L4 neurons consistently showed positive change coefficients, firing more spikes for deviant increases and fewer for decreases. This encoding is evident at the population level as a rightward shift in the distribution of change coefficients (Figure 7b, p=0.005, CI:[0.012, 0.016, 0.035]; See Figure 9—figure supplement 1 for generalized linear model 'GLM' analysis).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7b with statistical significance p=0.005.

claim: Spike count differences for deviations in L4 were larger than for equivalent variations in baseline amplitude with no deviant.
source: These spike count differences for deviations were larger than for equivalent variations in baseline amplitude with no deviant (p=0.016, signed rank).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with p=0.016.

claim: No significant deviant encoding was observed in L5.
source: We observed no significant deviant encoding in L5 (N = 92: p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing non-significant results (p>0.05).

claim: L4 findings can be interpreted as enhanced specificity of encoding following an adapting stimulus.
source: These findings in L4 can be interpreted as enhanced specificity of encoding following an adapting stimulus, as observed across several stimulus types (Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Moore et al., 1999; Andermann et al., 2004), in this case amplitude encoding.
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Moore et al., 1999; Andermann et al., 2004.

claim: The increased sensitivity of amplitude encoding in L4 after adaptation is consistent with enhanced discriminability of stimulus features generally observed with adaptation.
source: This increased sensitivity of amplitude encoding in L4 after adaptation to a baseline is consistent with the enhanced discriminability of stimulus features generally observed with adaptation (Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Békésy, 1967; Tannan et al., 2006; Abbott et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Békésy, 1967; Tannan et al., 2006; Abbott et al., 1997.

claim: A subset of L2/3 neurons showed positive change encoding, but negative change coefficients were also observed.
source: As in L4, a subset of L2/3 neurons showed positive change encoding, but negative change coefficients were also observed, i.e. neurons with greater firing in response to stimulus decreases (Figure 7a, examples ii and iii).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The L2/3 change coefficient distribution was significantly broader than the surrogate distribution.
source: The observed distribution was significantly broader than the surrogate (interquartile range/IQR; Figure 7c; p=0.006, Shannon entropy: p=0.029, via bootstrapping, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data in Figure 7c with p=0.006 for IQR and p=0.029 for entropy.

claim: L2/3 RS continued to represent change from stimulus history with a broadened distribution when deviant amplitude was fixed.
source: With fixed deviant amplitude, L2/3 RS continued to represent change from stimulus history with a broadened distribution (Figure 7d; IQR p=0.004, entropy p=0.014, N = 87), showing that L2/3 RS cells encode history dependent heterogeneous change signals.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7d with statistical significance.

claim: L2/3 RS cells encode history dependent heterogeneous change signals.
source: With fixed deviant amplitude, L2/3 RS continued to represent change from stimulus history with a broadened distribution (Figure 7d; IQR p=0.004, entropy p=0.014, N = 87), showing that L2/3 RS cells encode history dependent heterogeneous change signals.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of broadened distribution when deviant amplitude is fixed but preceded by different baseline amplitudes.

claim: L4 neurons encode deviant amplitude, reflected in a positive correlation between their rates and the direction of amplitude change.
source: In sum, L4 neurons encode deviant amplitude, reflected in a positive correlation between their rates and the direction of amplitude change.
evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claim: L2/3 neurons showed a variety of responses to deviants, with different receptive fields for specific patterns of baseline and deviant.
source: In contrast, L2/3 neurons showed a variety of responses to deviants, with different receptive fields for specific patterns of baseline and deviant (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7 showing heterogeneous responses.

claim: Only ~13% of L6 neurons were stimulus-driven in 2-photon imaging experiments.
source: Consistent with electrophysiological data, L6 activity was sparse, as only ~13% of L6 neurons were stimulus-driven (469/3408 cells, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: L6 CT cells encoded baseline amplitude, with significantly higher integrated calcium signals for larger stimuli.
source: When stimuli without deviants were presented, L6 CT cells encoded baseline amplitude, with significantly higher integrated calcium signals for larger stimuli (p<0.001 signed rank, N = 346, Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8 with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: L6 CT encoded amplitude differences when deviants were presented after 400 ms.
source: As with baseline amplitude variations, L6 CT also encoded these amplitude differences (p<0.001, Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8 with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: L6 CT encoded stimulus amplitude as a variation in relative firing rate, which could serve as a baseline for a change-detection computation.
source: Nevertheless, these data show that L6 CT encoded stimulus amplitude as a variation in relative firing rate, which could serve as a baseline for a change-detection computation.
evidence: Inferred from the amplitude encoding observed in L6 CT cells.

claim: Weak optogenetic drive removed the encoding of stimulus amplitude in L6 CT.
source: We found that weak optogenetic drive removed the encoding of stimulus amplitude (Figure 9d,e, p<0.05, ranksum, evoked ΔF/F change between stimuli, control vs. laser).
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 9d,e with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: Both the identity of the sensory-driven ensemble and amplitude encoding by L6 CT was disrupted by weak optogenetic drive.
source: In sum, both the identity of the sensory-driven ensemble and amplitude encoding by L6 CT was disrupted by weak optogenetic drive, despite no change in the net activity in these neurons.
evidence: Summary of findings from 2-photon imaging data in Figures 5, 8, and 9.

claim: Weak L6 CT drive caused a loss in the heterogeneity of L2/3 encoding of deviants.
source: Across the L2/3 population, weak L6 CT drive caused a loss in the heterogeneity of L2/3 encoding of deviants, reflected as a sharpening of the distribution and a bias to positive change coefficients, paralleling L4 encoding.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9b showing distribution changes.

claim: Change representation in L2/3 was disrupted by weak optogenetic drive of L6.
source: We found that change representation in L2/3 was disrupted (Figure 9b, p=0.010 entropy reduction, p=0.020 IQR reduction, p=0.008 paired left tailed IQR, N = 94).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9b with multiple statistical measures.

claim: During optogenetic drive, L2/3 neurons came to represent current stimulus amplitudes with positive change coefficients and reduced their history-dependence.
source: During optogenetic drive, L2/3 neurons came to represent current stimulus amplitudes with positive change coefficients (CI: [0.002, 0.009, 0.016], p=0.003 signed rank) and reduced their history-dependence (Figure 9, p=0.014 entropy reduction, p=0.004 IQR reduction, p=0.043 paired left tailed IQR).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9 with statistical significance.

claim: Shuffling the active L6 ensemble removed the change-specific receptive fields in L2/3, causing them to instead encode current stimuli, making them more similar to L4 cells.
source: Shuffling the active L6 ensemble therefore removed the change-specific receptive fields in L2/3, causing them to instead encode current stimuli, making them more similar to L4 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the shift in L2/3 encoding properties under weak L6 drive.

claim: Optogenetic drive of L6 impacts sensory responses in visual neocortex through an intracortical pathway, not by modulation of thalamic relay neurons.
source: Recent studies have concluded that optogenetic drive of L6 impacts sensory responses in visual neocortex through an intracortical pathway, and not by modulation of thalamic relay neurons (Olsen et al., 2012; Bortone et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Olsen et al., 2012 and Bortone et al., 2014.

claim: Of 240 well-isolated thalamic single units, 25 cells were phasically responsive at short latencies to vibrissal stimulation.
source: Of 240 well-isolated thalamic single units (N = 3 mice), 25 cells were phasically responsive at short latencies to vibrissal stimulation.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from VPM.

claim: VPM neurons showed weak rate increases with L6 optogenetic drive, in contrast to the suppression observed in prior studies using stronger L6 CT drive.
source: These neurons showed weak rate increases with L6 optogenetic drive, in contrast to the suppression observed in prior studies using stronger L6 CT drive (Denman and Contreras, 2015; Bortone et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data from VPM recordings and citations to Denman and Contreras, 2015 and Bortone et al., 2014.

claim: No significant encoding of deviants was observed in VPM, nor was modulation of encoding of deviants by L6 drive observed.
source: However, no significant encoding of deviants was observed, nor was modulation of encoding of deviants by L6 drive observed (Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: Layers that receive direct lemniscal thalamic input (L4, L5, and L6) did not show explicit deviance encoding other than encoding of current stimulus amplitude.
source: Further, as described above, layers that receive direct lemniscal thalamic input (L4, L5, and L6) did not show explicit deviance encoding other than encoding of current stimulus amplitude.
evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data across layers.

claim: Evidence supports a local neocortical mechanism for the emergence of L2/3 deviant responses and their modulation under L6 optogenetic drive.
source: These two forms of evidence, and prior studies finding a direct intracortical pathway as the primary route of influence by L6 CT (Bortone et al., 2014), supports a local neocortical mechanism for the emergence of L2/3 deviant responses and in their modulation under L6 optogenetic drive.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of lack of thalamic deviance encoding and prior studies, with citation to Bortone et al., 2014.

claim: Weak optogenetic drive of L6 CT substantially altered sensory encoding by L6 CT despite not altering overall firing rates.
source: However, this weak optogenetic stimulus regime did substantially alter sensory encoding by L6 CT. These neurons lost their amplitude encoding, and many individual neurons showed changes in their sensory responsiveness, shifting the specific ensemble of L6 CT activated (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5 showing ensemble changes and loss of encoding.

claim: L2/3 neurons lost their emergent heterogeneous encoding of deviants under weak L6 drive, showing instead the positive change encoding observed in L4 under normal conditions.
source: Further, L2/3 neurons lost their emergent heterogeneous encoding of deviants, showing instead the positive change encoding observed in L4 under normal conditions (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9.

claim: Weak L6 drive selectively suppressed indicators of deviant processing in head-fixed and free behaviors.
source: Weak L6 drive also selectively suppressed indicators of deviant processing in head-fixed (Figure 3) and free (Figures 1 and 2) behaviors.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: Layer-specific encoding of deviants was observed.
source: We observed layer-specific encoding of deviants and robust behavioral sensitivity to small stimulus deviations.
evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Robust behavioral sensitivity to small stimulus deviations was observed.
source: We observed layer-specific encoding of deviants and robust behavioral sensitivity to small stimulus deviations.
evidence: Summary of findings from behavioral data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Small stimulus amplitude deviants were correlated positively with firing rates in L4 and L6.
source: Small stimulus amplitude deviants were correlated positively with firing rates in L4 and L6, with deviant amplitude increases driving higher firing rates.
evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological and imaging data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Heterogeneous encoding emerged in L2/3 neurons, where cells could encode amplitude increases by decreases in rate.
source: In contrast, heterogeneous encoding, where cells could, for example, encode amplitude increases by decreases in rate, and encoding of stimulus history, emerged in L2/3 neurons.
evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claim: Encoding of stimulus history emerged in L2/3 neurons.
source: In contrast, heterogeneous encoding, where cells could, for example, encode amplitude increases by decreases in rate, and encoding of stimulus history, emerged in L2/3 neurons.
evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data in Figure 7d.

claim: Weak optogenetic drive changed the sensory-responsive L6 ensemble by facilitating and suppressing different subsets of cells without changing overall firing rates.
source: Weak optogenetic drive changed the sensory-responsive L6 ensemble, by facilitating and suppressing different subsets of cells without changing the overall firing rates and reduced their information content about the stimulus.
evidence: Summary of findings from 2-photon imaging data in Figures 5 and 8.

claim: Weak optogenetic drive reduced the information content of L6 about the stimulus.
source: Weak optogenetic drive changed the sensory-responsive L6 ensemble, by facilitating and suppressing different subsets of cells without changing the overall firing rates and reduced their information content about the stimulus.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Detection of small stimulus deviations in the Gap Crossing with Deviants task was lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance.
source: Detection of small stimulus deviations in the Gap Crossing with Deviants task, and the benefit of deviants for basic detection, were also lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance (Figure 10).
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings shown in Figure 10.

claim: The benefit of deviants for basic detection was lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance.
source: Detection of small stimulus deviations in the Gap Crossing with Deviants task, and the benefit of deviants for basic detection, were also lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance (Figure 10).
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings shown in Figure 10.

claim: Stimulus encoding by sparse ensembles in L6 contributes to the neocortical circuit that processes sensory deviation but is not required for basic sensory function.
source: These results indicate that stimulus encoding by sparse ensembles in L6 contributes to the neocortical circuit that processes sensory deviation but is not required for basic sensory function.
evidence: Inferred from the selective effects on deviant processing but not baseline performance.

claim: The weak L6 manipulation isolated a network mechanism or computation that is selectively involved in stimulus change processing, but not in processing of repeating, or predictable stimuli.
source: The specific impact of the weak L6 manipulation on deviant encoding but not sensory gain (Figures 4 and 9), and on deviant-driven sensory behaviors but not basic performance (Figures 2 and 3), indicates that this intervention isolated a network mechanism or computation that is selectively involved in stimulus change processing, but not in processing of repeating, or predictable stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of selective effects across multiple measures.

claim: The failure of weak L6 drive to impact baseline behavior contrasts with findings showing that subtle optogenetic manipulation in SI can affect baseline sensory detection behavior.
source: The failure of weak L6 drive to impact baseline behavior is in contrast with several findings showing that relatively subtle optogenetic manipulation in SI, for example induced via similarly weak drive of PV+ interneurons (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Siegle et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012) or L4 stellate neurons (O'Connor et al., 2013; Sofroniew et al., 2015), or direct stimulation of single neurons in other layers (Houweling and Brecht, 2008), can affect baseline sensory detection behavior.
evidence: Comparison to prior literature supported by citations to Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Siegle et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2013; Sofroniew et al., 2015; Houweling and Brecht, 2008.

claim: The stimulus design minimized stimulus-specific adaptation.
source: Here, we specifically sought to minimize such stimulus-specific adaptation.
evidence: Stated experimental design goal, supported by lack of overall rate increase for deviants (Figure 6e).

claim: The lack of stimulus-specific adaptation is evident in the lack of overall increase in firing rates for deviants.
source: This lack of stimulus-specific adaptation is evident in the lack of overall increase in firing rates for deviants (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6e.

claim: The L6 CT cells imaged and controlled may affect cortical activity via recruitment of local and trans-laminar FS mediated inhibition.
source: The L6 CT cells imaged and controlled in the present experiments may affect cortical activity via the recruitment of local (Zhang and Deschênes, 1997) and trans-laminar (Bortone et al., 2014) FS mediated inhibition, and through corticothalamic effects (Thomson, 2010; Denman and Contreras, 2015).
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to Zhang and Deschênes, 1997; Bortone et al., 2014; Thomson, 2010; Denman and Contreras, 2015.

claim: The L6 CT cells may affect cortical activity through corticothalamic effects.
source: The L6 CT cells imaged and controlled in the present experiments may affect cortical activity via the recruitment of local (Zhang and Deschênes, 1997) and trans-laminar (Bortone et al., 2014) FS mediated inhibition, and through corticothalamic effects (Thomson, 2010; Denman and Contreras, 2015).
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to Thomson, 2010 and Denman and Contreras, 2015.

claim: The mechanisms by which specific ensembles of L6 cells influence state or stimulus encoding in superficial layers are still largely unknown.
source: The mechanisms by which specific ensembles of L6 cells influence state or stimulus encoding in superficial layers are still largely unknown, and could also be mediated through a variety of intermediate cell types, layers, and brain areas that were not recorded in the present set of experiments.
evidence: Acknowledgment of knowledge gap.

claim: The present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the behavioral benefit of deviants.
source: While the present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the behavioral benefit of deviants, and in the representation of deviation across neocortical layers, further studies are required to determine the circuit, synaptic and cellular mechanisms by which L6 affects neural encoding and behavior.
evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claim: The present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the representation of deviation across neocortical layers.
source: While the present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the behavioral benefit of deviants, and in the representation of deviation across neocortical layers, further studies are required to determine the circuit, synaptic and cellular mechanisms by which L6 affects neural encoding and behavior.
evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claim: The encoding of small stimulus changes in L2/3 RS is analogous to the emergence of complex temporospatial receptive fields in upper layers of visual neocortex.
source: The encoding of small stimulus changes in L2/3 RS, specifically the history dependence of these responses, is analogous to the emergence of complex temporospatial receptive fields (Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Gilbert, 1977) and mismatch encoding (Zmarz and Keller, 2016) in upper layers of visual neocortex.
evidence: Comparison to prior literature supported by citations to Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Gilbert, 1977; Zmarz and Keller, 2016.

claim: The diversity in L2/3 responses could reflect neuron types defined by biophysical characteristics or projection targets.
source: The diversity in L2/3 responses, where both positive and negative change coefficients were observed, could reflect neuron types defined by biophysical characteristics (Jouhanneau et al., 2014) or projection targets, such as targeting higher somatosensory or motor cortices (Sato and Svoboda, 2010; Chen et al., 2013b), or may emerge from differential afferent connectivity.
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to Jouhanneau et al., 2014; Sato and Svoboda, 2010; Chen et al., 2013b.

claim: The sparsity of L6 CT activity and their targeting by long-range corticocortical afferents suggests they might be gated by inputs from other higher-order neocortical areas.
source: The sparsity of L6 CT activity, and their targeting by long-range corticocortical afferents (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014), suggests that they might be gated by inputs from other higher-order neocortical areas, as previously proposed (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to Vélez-Fort et al., 2014 and Lee et al., 2008.

claim: A sparse pattern of activity in L6, comprised of both active and inactive neurons with specific connectivity, is required for deviance encoding.
source: Even though weak L6 CT drive did not alter stimulus-driven firing rates, this manipulation changed the ensemble of sensory-driven neurons. This finding suggests that a sparse pattern of activity, comprised of both active and inactive neurons in L6, with specific connectivity, is required for deviance encoding.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of ensemble shuffling on deviance encoding.

claim: The specific population of L6 cells active during optogenetic drive was different from the one active in control conditions.
source: There are two types of mechanisms by which this manipulation could lead to the observed disruption of change encoding in L2/3. The specific population of L6 cells active during optogenetic drive was different from the one active in control conditions.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5.

claim: The population of L6 CT cells that is active during optogenetic drive carries less stimulus information than the population that is active in the control condition.
source: Additionally, we found that the population of L6 CT cells that is active during optogenetic drive carries less stimulus information than the population that is active in the control condition (Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2), suggesting that any decoding of stimulus information from L6 would be impaired under the optogenetic drive condition.
evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The findings do not provide evidence for or against a specific circuit or circuits for change detection.
source: Regardless of mechanism, our findings do not provide evidence for or against a specific circuit or circuits for change detection, but rather that specific activity patterns in L6 are required for the cortical architecture to perform change detection.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitations in interpretation.

claim: Specific activity patterns in L6 are required for the cortical architecture to perform change detection.
source: Regardless of mechanism, our findings do not provide evidence for or against a specific circuit or circuits for change detection, but rather that specific activity patterns in L6 are required for the cortical architecture to perform change detection.
evidence: Inferred from the necessity of specific L6 ensembles for deviance encoding and behavior.

claim: The similar findings across Gap Crossing and head-fixed paradigms suggest the mechanism could be involved in more general predictive models.
source: In this study, we employed two kinds of deviants. Variations from repeating baseline stimuli applied to the vibrissae, and ethologically relevant deviations in the position of a platform in the middle of sampling by freely behaving animals. In the latter case, the stimulus statistics (mainly vibrissa identity, angles, and curvature upon touch) change continuously as the mice approach or retreat from the target platform (Voigts et al., 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 2). In both cases, predictive models were at some level formed within the system, driving the change in response patterns and behavior. The similar findings across these paradigms suggests that the mechanism underlying the observed effects could be involved in more general predictive models.
evidence: Inferred from consistency of findings across different behavioral paradigms.

claim: L6 CT could be one node of the larger laminar cortical circuit for processing of higher-order stimulus features, stimulus context, or expectations reliant on top-down signaling.
source: In sum, we found that stimulus encoding by specific ensembles of L6 cells is required for change encoding in L2/3 and for change-detection behavior, but not basic detection performance. These L6 CT could therefore be one node of the larger laminar cortical circuit for processing of higher-order stimulus features, stimulus context, or expectations reliant on top-down signaling, in agreement with L6 CT targeting by long-range cortico-cortical inputs (Zhang et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from findings and supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018.

claim: NTSR1-Cre mice were used in the experiments.
source: NTSR1-Cre mice (strain B6.FVB(Cg)-Tg(Ntsr1-cre)GN220Gsat/Mmcd, stock number 030648-UCD) (Gong et al., 2007) of either sex were used.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects with citation to Gong et al., 2007.

claim: For some experiments, NTSR1-Cre mice were crossed with a floxed ChR2 reporter line.
source: For some experiments, NTSR1-Cre mice were crossed with a floxed ChR2 reporter line (strain B6;129S-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm32(CAG-COP4*H134R/EYFP)Hze/J, stock number 012569).
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: AAV DIO ChR2-mCherry was used for virus mediated ChR2 expression.
source: 300 nl of virus (AAV DIO ChR2-mCherry;~2 × 10^12 viral molecules per ml) was injected at 0.05 μl/min at ~800 μm below the dura.
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: AAV2/1-hSyn-Flex-GCaMP6s was used for two-photon imaging.
source: For two- photon imaging,~300 nl of AAV2/1-hSyn-Flex-GCaMP6s (HHMI/Janelia Farm, GENIE Project; ~1 × 10^13 viral molecules per ml) (Chen et al., 2013a), or in a subset of mice a 1:1 mixture of floxed GCaMP6 and floxed ChR2, all produced by the U. Penn Vector Core, was injected at ~750 μm targeting the posterior c-row barrels, identified by vascular landmarks and confirmed using intrinsic imaging to restrict expression to NTSR1+ neurons.
evidence: Description of experimental methods with citation to Chen et al., 2013a.

claim: Mice with fluorescent non-L6 cells were excluded from the study.
source: Mice were tested for aberrant expression outside of L6 CT cells either by histology (for behavior and electrophysiology), or by collecting z-stacks (for 2-photon imaging). Mice with fluorescent non-L6 cells were excluded from the study.
evidence: Description of experimental quality control.
